newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court rejects gays-in-military appeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court rejects gays-in-military appeal.

text.p: The Supreme Court Monday rejected a constitutional challenge to President Clinton's "don't ask, don't tell" policy that allows gays to be discharged from the military.
The action marked the second time the high court has refused to get involved in the legal battles surrounding the policy. In October, it turned down a similar appeal in another case.
The Clinton administration put the policy into effect after Congress in 1993 adopted a law relaxing the military's 50-year prohibition on homosexuals serving in the military.

Under the compromise reached between Congress and the administration, the military cannot question members or recruits about their sexual orientation, but overt homosexual acts or statements can lead to discharge.
The case involved Richard Dirk Selland, a former Navy lieutenant who had been assinged to a nuclear submarine.

After crew members joked about his homosexuality, Selland in 1993 consulted a Navy chaplain and told him he was gay. On the chaplain's advice, he then revealed his sexual orientation to the ship's commanding officer.
Selland was immediately ordered off the ship and later was discharged from the Navy.

Selland sued, saying the policy violated the constitutional equal protection guarantee and free-speech rights because his discharge had been based solely on statements made in private to a chaplain and his commanding officer.
A federal judge and a U.S. appeals court ruled against Selland. He asked the Supreme Court to hear the case, but the justices denied the request without any comment or dissent.
